rationale: The cited texts portray the new moon as a recurring monthly cultic feast and observance (trumpets, royal meals, temple worship, commerce pause) that Colossians classifies among ceremonial shadows fulfilled in Christ. They supply no statement equating chodesh with the full-moon phase, relocating month-start to fullness, or placing the lunar disk itself inside Ezekiel’s temple east gate. The strongest counter-reading accounts for every detail with ordinary calendrical usage of chodesh (month-beginning at dark/crescent) plus the separate term keseh, without phase identity or calendar reversal. Psalm 81:3’s parallelism is more naturally new-moon plus appointed/full-moon feast marker than forced synonymy; Ezekiel’s gate opening is for worship access on the new-moon day, not an astronomical entry description. The book’s full-moon identification therefore adds unsupported steps and does not explain the evidence better.
book_core_identification: The new moon (renewed moon) is the full-moon phase that marks the start of the month, stands in the east gate, and functions as the sign of the appointed times.
book_secondary_elaborations: The phase of the moon that marks the start of the month
unsupported_glossary_assertions: The phase that marks the start of the month is the full moon
The full moon in the east gate
Sign of the appointed times (as the full-moon new moon)
chapter_only_objections: Pearl = full-moon bride purchased by the merchant-Son, with pearl-gates as moedim
Reconstructed calendar in which the month begins at full moon (and major feast datings must be re-mapped)
Temple east-gate opening equated to the full moon’s rise as ‘entry by the door’ versus the crescent as thief
strongest_counter_interpretation: The new moon is the ordinary calendrical and cultic observance that begins each lunar month at the moon’s dark or first-crescent renewal, marked by feasts, trumpets, offerings and rest from commerce, and treated by Colossians as a shadow whose substance belongs to Christ.
counter_core_identification: Start-of-month ceremonial day (chodesh) in Israel’s calendar, a shadow fulfilled in Christ.
material_core_denial: The new moon is not the full-moon phase; fullness (keseh) is a distinct mid-month marker, while chodesh begins the month at lunar renewal in darkness or crescent.
counter_case: Ps 81:3 parallels chodesh and keseh/appointed time on the feast day without equating the two phases
1 Sam 20:5, 18 simply schedules a new-moon royal feast at month-start with no phase data favoring fullness
Ezek 46:1-3 opens the temple’s east gate for worship on new-moon days exactly as on sabbaths, not because the moon disk enters a sky gate
Isa 66:23, Amos 8:5 and Col 2:16-17 treat new moons as regular cycle markers or shadows alongside holydays and sabbaths, fitting standard monthly observance
No supplied text asserts that the month begins at full moon or that ‘new moon’ means full moon
book_explanatory_advantages: Notes the astronomical fact that a full moon rises in the east near nightfall
Connects the moon generally to signs and moedim (though the texts do not restrict this to full moon as new moon)
counter_explanatory_advantages: Preserves the ordinary lexical distinction between chodesh and keseh
Fits every cited verse with standard Hebrew calendrical usage and known new-moon customs
Requires no redefinition of month-start or phase identity
Aligns directly with Colossians’ shadow category for the ceremonial calendar triad
Explains feast, trumpet and commerce references as ordinary first-of-month practice
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Ps 81:3’s parallel phrasing most naturally keeps chodesh and keseh/appointed time distinct or associated rather than identical phases
Absence of any explicit claim in the supplied texts that new moon = full moon or that the month begins at fullness
Col 2:16-17’s grouping of new moon with holydays and sabbaths as shadows, carrying no full-moon or east-gate imagery
unresolved_objections: Eastward full-moon rise could still supply poetic color to new-moon temple liturgy under a standard phase reading
